title: The Light of Home
paragraphs: The home is all music;
The hearts of the inmates all are things lustrous; Their minds are all books of knowledge; The letters of the books are marks of joy; The woods are a spectacle of dance.
If it is so for crows, sparrows and cows Need we say anything about men?
The revolutionary poet Pāratitācaṉ’s picture of a home it is! And our ripe author of antiquity Tolkāppiyar Has drawn a similar picture two thousand years ago.
The Poruḷatikāram, Karpiyal section of Tolkāppiyam Shows the two lamps at home That like blossoms of a creeper diffuse fragrance around.
The wedded life sweet suffers no want as it were; And yet the man tells his parrot-tongued wife, “Don’t you feel the want of a child at home?”
A pointed finger was her reply to his concern. “Stop there! Are you threatening me?” Said the man in mocking jest “It has been a month since the period stopped”, said she.
With a joyous roar of laughter He took her in his clasp Her resistance notwithstanding.

“Mind your health, my dear! Conceived, you need to take much care,” Cautioning her thus, He kept moving behind her all through From month one to the ninth month of her pregnancy With care and concern undiminished.
He parted from her with a sigh As the midwife came to attend to childbirth.
As he heard the words ‘male child’ from the labour room He went about dancing in rapture.
Allowed to see his wife, he went in And all her pain vanished without a trace. The flower of that woman wore a smile Holding the bud of the baby close to her.

He wiped the sweat on her forehead, Saying, “You are reduced much like a twig, dear!” She blushed for a while And said with a streak of ridicule at the corner of her eyes: “Reduced in just one day’s pain?”
She was showered in benediction by all kindred folk, Her parents and foster mother in particular. All kindly people thronged to greet her.
She was bathed in oil. There was a celebration for the child
When the martyrs who sacrificed for the freedom of the land Were remembered with grateful admiration. The lady was floating on the ocean of joy.
Then she heard the tidings of her man Drawn in passion to an alien woman.
It was a blow as if by an axe; She writhed in pain like a worm thrown into fire.
He was worried about Her turning a tiger and a storm. The hill-like man stood reduced in his standing.
He approached her companions With a request to quench The raging fire in the heart of the heroine. The efforts of them came to no avail.
Eventually, He went to her in the bedchamber Held her legs in tight hold And begged her pardon.
Could she say ‘no’ to him? Or could she erase his image from her mind? She did pardon him.
“May the one who coined the word ‘pardon’ live long!” Thinking thus The hero moved closer to her And she moved off a little Saying, “There is the child!”
> Bearing him a son worthy of his name; > > As gifts aplenty are bestowed on the sages > And worthy offerings on the celestials > At the hour of the heroine

> Being given the ceremonial oil-bath > After she has borne him a son; > > As he comes after acts of debauchery > And entreats the bliss of heroine’s love > Holding her tender feet in his hands, > While she in a mood of variance > Stays lying despondent on the bed > With the soft pillow for her prop; > > As he brings in the intercession of other women > And resolves the sulking of the heroine > When she remains hard of access > In a mode of intense variance; > > .... > > (Poruḷatikāram : Karpiyal, verse 5)
